Subject
Selection of Chair and Vice Chair

Recommendation
Select one member to serve as Chairperson and one member to serve as Vice Chairperson for
the term ending on June 30, 2026.
Background
The Business and Industry Commission (Commission) consists of seven members, including
three Business Representatives, one Council Member, one individual employed by a business
in Vernon or a Labor Representative, and two Real Estate Representatives. Members serve a
term of four years and may be reappointed. Members serve no more than two consecutive full
four-year terms.

Pursuant to Vernon Municipal Code (VMC) Section 2.52.100.B., members are required to elect
a Chairperson and Vice Chairperson annually from different appointing categories under Section
2.52.050. Additionally, a member may not serve as Chairperson for more than two consecutive
terms. The VMC is silent on term limits for the Vice Chairperson.

On September 12, 2024, the Commission selected Commissioner Condon to serve his first
annual term as Chairperson. On September 12, 2024, the Commission selected Commissioner
Morfin to serve his second annual term as Vice Chairperson.
The current members are as follows:

1.  Fiscal Year 2025-26 Proposed Budget Overview
  Recommendation:
  No action required by Commission. This is a presentation only.
  City Administrator Saeki introduced the new City Clerk, Genoveva Rocha and newly
  appointed Finance Director Alice Hui to the Commissioners.

  City Administrator Saeki presented the staff report and accompanying PowerPoint
  presentation.
  In response to questions from the Commission, Staff provided additional information
  on the budget, they explained how staff defined transfers out of the electric fund and
  the costs for services such as payroll and benefits administration.

  Staff also provided the Commission with additional information on the budget for
  maintenance and operations, capital investment projects, utility transmission line, the
  addition of an additional water well, and prioritizing hydrant flushing as a lesson learned
  from the Eaton and Palisades fires.

  In response to the Commission’s questions on revenue impacts related to the data
  center and the loss of some major customers, VPU staff provided information on the
  City Council approval of the strategy to stabilize the billing component on customers’
  energy bill over three years, adding that along with the anticipated developments, the
  overall load will increase and in turn, increase the revenues.

  Commission members expressed concerns over increasing inflation rates, lower rental
  rates and calculations of the parcel tax as it relates to CPI and provided perspectives
  on vacancy rates, surcharges, warehousing vacancies, decreasing imports, increasing
  tariffs, parcel tax, and economic impacts surrounding warehousing in the City. The
  Commission requested a different look at options related to the calculations of the
  warehouse parcel tax.

  In response to concerns voiced by Commission members regarding whether the City's
  energy rate chart encompasses all fees and utility taxes, VPU staff provided information
  on comparative energy usage as it relates to other cities that have far greater residential
  customers and the unique and largely industrial base in Vernon.
  Vice Chair Morfin inquired about the City's fiscal responsibility concerning PFAS
  cleanups. City Administrator Saeki explained that the responsibility falls to each City
  while leveraging our State and Federal partners to help fund related projects. Public
  Utilities Assistant General Manager Otto shared that VPU closely monitors its drinking
  water for contaminants and has well monitoring.

  Chair Condon invited public comments. There being none, Agenda Item No. 2 was
  introduced.

Item 2  Page 7 of 27
 Regular Business and Industry Commission Meeting Minutes  Page 3 of 4
May 8, 2025

2.  Business License Tax
  Recommendation:
  No action required by Commission. This is a presentation only.

  City Administrator Saeki presented the staff report and Deputy City Treasurer Leon
  conducted a PowerPoint presentation.
  In response to Commission questions related to property square footage for business
  warehousing, Deputy City Treasurer Leon confirmed there is a cap on the business
  license tax and provided the average tax for the most recent annual renewal season
  was $5,777. It was clarified the average square footage per location, or user was
  calculated at approximately 24,000 square feet.

  The Commission members discussed the differences between manufacturing and
  warehousing, adding assembly to the process, shared some of the history of the
  warehouse tax which used to be miniscule and then presented challenges for business
  property owners once the tax was significantly increased. The Commission expressed
  interest in attracting new businesses to the City and thought it would help to simplify
  the tax calculation on the hybrid model.

  In response to a question on the definition of non-warehousing, Deputy City Treasurer
  Leon explained that the non-warehousing portion of a warehouse tax would include the
  area designated as office space, assembly area and staging and when an inspector
  visits the warehouse, the inspector would determine the square footage and then note
  the non-warehousing areas and consider the location’s unique situation.

  The Commission expressed concerns over the business tax on multiple locations, staff
  explained that according to business license records relating to the hybrid model, the
  City has two businesses that have four locations, two businesses that have three
  locations, and several businesses that have two locations. Staff explained there are
  factors that impact the calculations of business license tax depending on the type of
  license a business has.

  The Commission inquired about business tax on multiple adjacent locations compared
  to multiple non-adjacent locations, staff explained the business license tax is codified
  and to change the process would require approval by the City Council to take a ballot
  to the voters to amend the code.
  Police Chief Sousa provided information on copper wire theft in response to questions
  from the Commission.

  Chair Condon invited public comments.

  The Commission inquired and staff discussed and determined the average tax was
  $1,800 for businesses that were taxed based on the number of employees.

  Wednesday, May 14th, at the Vernon Chamber of Commerce 2025 Economic Forecast
  and Industry Update Luncheon at Bridgepoint in Vernon. He stated speakers from U.S.
  Bank and L.A. Economic Development Corporation would provide an outlook on the
  regional labor market, global tariff climate and impacts on U.S. businesses and would
  provide the status of California and the regional economy.

  Lastly, he extended an invitation to the upcoming E-Waste Event in which Arion Global,
  and our Department of Health and Environmental Control would be co-hosting the
  annual electronic and universal waste recycling event at the Leonis Substation on 50th
  Street on Thursday, May 22nd from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. He encouraged all to
  support the effort to keep dangerous contaminants like lead, mercury and arsenic out
  of landfills and away from water supplies by recycling unused or obsolete electronics.

Meeting Date:  October 2, 2025
From:  Todd Dusenberry, General Manager of Public Utilities
Department:  Public Utilities
Submitted by:  Adriana Ramos, Senior Management Analyst

Subject
Vernon Public Utilities Water Rate Study

Recommendation
Receive and file the report on the Vernon Public Utilities Water Rate Study.

Background
A Cost of Service (COS) Study is an essential analytical tool that utilities use to develop rates
reflecting the actual cost components associated with each customer rate class. It is considered
best practice for utilities to conduct a COS every five years, a standard that many nearby public
utilities follow. The most recent Water COS and Rate Design Study for Vernon Public Utilities
(VPU) was completed in 2019.

To set appropriate rates that satisfy stakeholder business requirements, while ensuring that only
the necessary operating and capital costs for the Utility's operation and management are
included in VPU's rates, VPU requested approval from the City Council on February 4, 2025, for
an agreement with NewGen Strategies & Solutions, LLC (NewGen). This agreement provides
VPU with utility cost of service analysis, rate design, financial planning services, and
recommendations for adjustments to its rates.

This study allows VPU to make informed decisions and recommendations about Utility finance,
operations and future capital investments, while clearly understanding customer affordability,
competitiveness, cost constraints and the steps required to stabilize expenses in a fluctuating
global economic environment.

VPU staff will be presenting the results of the Water Fund COS, which is in compliance with
Proposition 218. Enacted in 1996, Proposition 218 mandates that public utility service rates, fees,
and charges must be reasonable and proportional to the costs of providing those services. This
means that the approach to setting rates must be sound, with a clear connection between the
costs incurred and the rates charged. VPU plans to present the results of the COS Study and
proposed Water rate adjustments to the City Council in the coming weeks.

Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report.

  Public Utilities General Manager Dusenberry presented the staff report and

 Docusign Envelope ID: DA323533-A6A0-40AF-AEAC-699EE9617D7C

  The Commission expressed interest in prospective growth and usage for the new data
  centers and hydrogen plant, and the revenue loss of the mentioned top-ten user
  (rPlanet Earth). Staff explained the prospective usage of the clean hydrogen and data
  centers would increase load, but combined, would not replace the usage of Farmer
  John.

  Public Utilities General Manager Dusenberry explained one of the reasons behind
  Vernon’s water rates being low in comparison to other agencies is that the utility
  understands the water rate directly hits businesses’ bottom line, and the increase
  actually supports the utility keeping the rates lower in comparison to the expensive and
  uncontrollable cost of importing water.

  Staff provided information on reclaimed water usage and demand, and explained
  reclaimed water used at the power plant is provided by Central Basin and the use of
  reclaimed water could be expanded in the future, noting that the reclaimed water
  system is not built out, and the price of building the infrastructure would be costly.

  Staff explained the transfer from the Electric Fund to the Water Fund is capped at $15
  million, and the imported water cost and average noted in the presentation is over the
  past 5 years.

  In response to questions from the Commission on the availability of ground water in
  drought conditions, staff explained in past droughts, Vernon’s ground water wells met
  the water usage demands without having to import water adding Vernon’s ground water
  wells have supplied 100% of the water in Vernon since November 2020 and, although
  Central Basin’s water connection valves are routinely flushed, they are exercised as a
  back-up water source for the City.

  Staff explained ground water well depths and prospective treatment plans, a minor
  detection for PFAS, grant funding availability, briefed on lawsuit settlement fund
  sources, and expanded on information on the process of recharging ground water wells
  which are mainly performed by Public Works operations through different storm water
  capture systems, and new construction development requirements.

  Staff explained the proposed water rate does not include taxes or other fees such as
  pass-through fees.

  In response to the Commission’s interest in incentivizing big businesses and large
  water consumers to the City, Staff explained the utility applies the rate objectively and
  evenly to large and small users alike. Staff added that Vernon has ownership rights to
  all the ground water in Vernon and has the capacity to provide water service to any size
  business such as the former dye-houses that were formerly located in Vernon.

  Staff provided information on the proposed rate-roll out plan to perform outreach and
  opportunity for the public to make comments would be somewhat flexible, would include

  City Administrator Saeki announced that in support of the Vernon community workers
  and businesses, the City has created a webpage dedicated to immigration and
  enforcement resources and has partnered with CHIRLA (Coalition for Humane
  Immigrant Rights) to provide legal support services and education. He added that
  CHIRLA would be hosting weekly virtual immigration training sessions for Vernon
  businesses and workers every Thursday at 3 p.m. alternating week to week in English
  and Spanish.

  He also announced October is “Pink Patch Project Month” recognizing breast cancer
  awareness during the month of October. Chief Sousa has authorized uniformed
  personnel to wear pink patches throughout the month of October to raise funds for the
  Pink Patch Project, an organization dedicated to raising breast cancer awareness and
  supporting research and prevention. He added this year’s Pink Patch Project gear
  would be available for sale to the public; patches would be available to purchase for
  $10 and Pink Patch Project t-shirts would be available to purchase for $20. Anyone
  interested in purchasing patches and t-shirts could contact Detective Gonzalez at
